name: AT25256B-SSHL-T
title: 128 Kbit and 256 Kbit SPI serial EEPROM
summary: The AT25128B and AT25256B are serial EEPROMs of 131,072 and 262,144 bits, arranged as 16,384 or 32,768 bytes, reached over an SPI bus in mode 0 or mode 3 at up to 20 MHz from a 5 V supply. They run from 1.8 V to 5.5 V, write single bytes or 64-byte pages in a self-timed cycle of at most 5 ms with no erase step, and protect a quarter, a half or all of the array through status register bits, backed by a hardware WP pin. A HOLD pin pauses a transfer without ending it.
key_figures: 20 MHz max at 4.5–5.5 V; 10 MHz at 2.5–5.5 V; 5 MHz at 1.8–5.5 V
0.2 µA typ at 1.8 V, 2 µA typ at 5.0 V

notes: (1) B suffix: shipped in tubes, 100 per tube for SOIC and TSSOP.
(2) T suffix: tape and reel, 4,000 per reel for SOIC; 5,000 per reel for TSSOP, UDFN and VFBGA.
(3) Wafer parts are sold through Atmel sales.

Order code key: AT, then 25 for the standard SPI family, density 128 or 256, device revision B; package SS = JEDEC SOIC, X = TSSOP, MA = UDFN, C = VFBGA, WWU = unsawn wafer, WDT = die in tape and reel; grade H = green with NiPdAu lead finish, industrial range (-40°C to +85°C), U = green with matte Sn lead finish, industrial range, 11 = 11 mil wafer thickness; voltage L = 1.8V to 5.5V; shipping B or blank = bulk (tubes), T = tape and reel.

Package codes: 8S1 is an 8-lead 0.15" wide plastic gull-wing SOIC (JEDEC); 8X is an 8-lead TSSOP with a 4.40mm body; 8MA2 is an 8-pad UDFN, 2.00mm x 3.00mm body, 0.50mm pitch; 8U2-1 is an 8-ball VFBGA, 2.35mm x 3.73mm body, 0.75mm pitch.

circuits.title: Four devices on one SPI bus
circuits.description: A microcontroller as SPI master drives four memories. SI, SO and SCK of every memory are bused to the master's MOSI, MISO and clock; each memory gets its own select line from the master (SS0 to SS3) on its CS pin. A deselected memory holds its SO in high impedance.
notes: The memories may be AT25128B or AT25256B.

operation.text: The part accepts SPI mode 0 (CPOL 0, CPHA 0) and mode 3 (CPOL 1, CPHA 1). Timing is specified in mode 0.
SCK is only ever an input, so the device is always a slave. Data enters on SI and leaves on SO, most significant bit first, both for the opcode and for addresses and data.

Every instruction begins with CS falling. The first byte clocked in after that is the opcode. While CS is high the device ignores SI and keeps SO in high impedance. An unknown opcode makes the device ignore the rest of the transfer, with SO in high impedance, until CS falls again.

With the device selected and a transfer under way, taking HOLD low while SCK is low freezes the transfer; SO floats and SI is ignored, though SCK may keep running. Taking HOLD high again while SCK is low resumes the transfer where it stopped.

With WP high, reads and writes behave normally. With WP low and WPEN = 1, the status register cannot be written; WP falling while CS is still low aborts a pending status register write, but has no effect once the internal write cycle has begun. With WPEN = 0 the WP pin is ignored, so a board may tie WP to ground and still write the status register.

After power-up the device is write disabled. Each write (WRITE or WRSR) must be preceded by WREN, issued with WP high. WRDI clears the latch whatever WP is doing. The latch clears itself again at the end of every write cycle.

RDSR returns the status register: RDY shows a write cycle in progress, WEN the write enable latch, BP1 and BP0 the protected block, WPEN the hardware protect enable. WRSR writes BP1, BP0 and WPEN, which are nonvolatile and take a write cycle like array bytes.

The array is split into four segments; BP1 and BP0 select none, the top quarter, the top half or the whole array as read-only. When WP is low and WPEN is 1, the status register (BP bits and WPEN) and the protected blocks are locked and only unprotected blocks accept writes; WPEN cannot be cleared again while WP stays low. Hardware write protection is off whenever WP is high or WPEN is 0.

Drop CS, send the READ opcode and the two address bytes on SI; the byte at that address then shifts out on SO, and SI is ignored. Keeping CS low and clocking on returns successive bytes, the address counting up and wrapping from the top of the array to address 0, so one READ can return the whole memory. Raise CS to end.

With WP high and the latch set by WREN, drop CS, send WRITE, two address bytes and one or more data bytes. CS must rise during the SCK low time right after the last data bit (D0); that rising edge starts the self-timed write cycle (tWC, 5 ms max). Addresses inside a protected block are not written. If WP is low or WREN was not issued, the instruction is ignored when CS rises and the device returns to standby.

Up to 64 bytes go in one WRITE. After each byte the low six address bits step by one while the upper bits stay fixed, so more than 64 bytes wrap round to the start of that page and overwrite the first bytes sent.
During an internal write cycle only RDSR is accepted. RDY (bit 0) reads 1 while the cycle runs and 0 when it has finished.

SI is sampled on the rising edge of SCK (setup tSU, hold tH); SO changes after the falling edge of SCK (valid within tV, held for tHO) and floats tDIS after CS rises. CS must stay high for tCS between instructions, fall tCSS before the first SCK rise, and rise no sooner than tCSH after the last SCK fall. HOLD changes no sooner than tHD after an SCK fall and at least tCD before the next SCK rise; SO floats within tHZ of HOLD falling and drives again within tLZ of HOLD rising.
The fastest clock depends on the supply: 20 MHz needs 4.5 V to 5.5 V, 10 MHz needs 2.5 V to 5.5 V, and 5 MHz is allowed down to 1.8 V.
